It drives the nose wheel centre lock assembly.
items.explanation: The retraction actuator is a hydraulically operated line replaceable unit of the extension and retraction subsystem which retracts and extends the nose landing gear. It also serves as the drag brace, comprising an internal mechanical locking device.
references: AW189 RFM Section 7 — Landing Gear, Chap 32 (p.7-180)

items.question: What type is the AW189 nose landing gear shock absorber?
options: A double stage type with a low pressure and a high pressure chamber, integrated in the shock strut.
A single stage oleo-pneumatic strut with a separate nitrogen accumulator.
A rubber-in-compression stack inside the sliding tube.
A double stage type using two separate struts in series.
items.explanation: The NLG shock absorber is integrated in the shock strut. It is a double stage type with a low and a high pressure chamber.
references: AW189 RFM Section 7 — Landing Gear, Chap 32 (p.7-180)

items.question: What does the AW189 emergency switch position indicator show?
options: UNLCK amber for unlocked, UNLCK amber and blinking for armed, and LOCK green for locked.
UNLCK red for unlocked, amber for armed and green for locked.
OFF for unlocked, amber for armed and green for locked.
UNLCK amber for armed, blinking amber for unlocked and green for locked.
items.explanation: The emergency switch/position indicator shows UNLCK amber for the unlocked position, UNLCK amber and blinking for the armed position, and LOCK green for the locked position. The nose wheel centerlock indicator uses the same scheme.
references: AW189 RFM Section 7 — Landing Gear, Chap 32 (p.7-180)

items.question: What does the AW189 Environmental Control System do, and what does it include?
options: It heats, cools and treats the air used to ventilate and condition the cockpit, cabin and avionic equipment, and includes heating and forced ventilation, distribution, and an optional air purification system.
It conditions the cabin only — cockpit and avionics are cooled by ram air.
It provides heating and pressurisation for the cockpit and cabin.
It provides forced ventilation only; heating comes from a separate combustion heater.
items.explanation: The Environmental Control System gives a means of heating, cooling and treating the air used for ventilation and conditioning of the cockpit, the cabin and the avionic equipment. It includes the heating and forced ventilation system, the distribution system, and the optional air purification system.
references: AW189 RFM Section 7 — Environmental Control, Chap 21 (p.7-15)

items.question: What do the APU and ENG positions of the AW189 AIR COND/HEATER selector do?
options: In both, air conditioning is not operative and heating runs — with the APU as bleed-air source in APU, and the engines as bleed-air source in ENG.
They select which source drives the air conditioning compressor.
APU runs heating on the ground and ENG runs it in flight, with air conditioning available in both.
They select the electrical supply for the ECS fans, not the bleed source.
items.explanation: In the APU position air conditioning is not operative and the heating is operative with the APU as bleed-air source. In the ENG position air conditioning is not operative and the heating is operative with the engines as bleed-air source.
references: AW189 RFM Section 7 — Environmental Control, Chap 21 (p.7-17)

items.question: What happens with the AW189 AIR COND/HEATER selector at OFF?
options: The air conditioning system is not operative and the system works in ventilation mode only, according to the VENT switch.
The whole ECS shuts down, including ventilation.
Heating continues automatically using engine bleed air.
The system reverts to automatic temperature control using ram air.
items.explanation: With the selector OFF the air conditioning system is not operative; the system works in ventilation mode only, according to the VENT switch.
references: AW189 RFM Section 7 — Environmental Control, Chap 21 (p.7-17)

items.question: How do the AUTO and MAN positions of the AW189 temperature selector differ?
options: AUTO works for heating and air conditioning and controls supply temperature automatically per selector position; MAN is for heating only and gives the crew direct control.
AUTO is for air conditioning only and MAN is for both heating and cooling.
AUTO controls cabin temperature and MAN controls cockpit temperature.
AUTO is available in flight only; MAN is the ground mode.
items.explanation: AUTO is for heating and air conditioning modes and automatically controls air supply temperature as required by the selector position between cold and warm. MAN is used for heating only and gives the crew direct control.
references: AW189 RFM Section 7 — Environmental Control, Chap 21 (p.7-17)

items.question: How many cautions and advisories can the AW189 ECS present on the CAS?
options: Four cautions and four advisories.
Two cautions and six advisories.
Four cautions and no advisories.
Ten cautions and two advisories.
items.explanation: The status of the ECS components is shown in the PWR PLANT format, in the HELO display and in the CAS window, and the CAS window can list four cautions and four advisories.
references: AW189 RFM Section 7 — Environmental Control, Chap 21 (p.7-15)

items.question: What does the AW189 indicating/recording system include?
options: Instrument and control panels, the central warning and caution system, independent instruments and recorder systems.
The primary flight displays, multifunction displays and the standby instrument only.
The crew alerting system and the health and usage monitoring system only.
Independent instruments and recorders only — panels are covered under avionics.
items.explanation: The indicating/recording system includes instrument and controls panels, the central warning and caution system, independent instruments, and recorder systems.
references: AW189 RFM Section 7 — Indicating/Recording, Chap 31 (p.7-163)

items.question: Where is the AW189 standby magnetic compass installed?
options: On a support attached at the centre of the glareshield with four screws.
On the cockpit roof above the interseat console.
On the left windscreen pillar, clear of the instrument panel.
In the overhead console beside the circuit breaker panels.
items.explanation: The magnetic compass is installed on a support that is attached at the centre of the glareshield with four screws. It detects and shows the helicopter heading with reference to magnetic north, and consists of a rotating compass card.
references: AW189 RFM Section 7 — Indicating/Recording, Chap 31 (p.7-163)

items.question: What modes does the AW189 chronometer provide?
options: Local time in 12 hour format, UTC in 24 hour format, flight time and a stop watch — both timers counting up to 99 hours 59 minutes 59 seconds.
Local time and UTC only, both in 24 hour format.
Flight time and stop watch only, each limited to 9 hours 59 minutes.
Local time, UTC and elapsed time, with elapsed time limited to 60 minutes.
items.explanation: The chronometer provides local time of day in 12 hour format, UTC in 24 hour format, flight time accumulating up to 99 hours 59 minutes 59 seconds, and a stop watch counting up to 99 hours 59 minutes 59 seconds. Both the flight time and the stop watch continue to run when the chronometer is in other modes.
references: AW189 RFM Section 7 — Indicating/Recording, Chap 31 (p.7-163, 7-164)

items.question: What range does the AW189 outside air temperature indication cover, and where is the probe?
options: From -70 to +50 °C, from a stand-alone probe situated outside the top right laminated window.
From -55 to +70 °C, from a probe in the forward inlet of the number 1 engine.
From -70 to +50 °C, from a probe under the nose beside the pitot masts.
From -40 to +60 °C, from a probe in the left sponson leading edge.
items.explanation: The outside air temperature sensor uses a stand alone temperature probe and indicates a temperature from -70 to +50 °C. The temperature probe is situated outside the top right laminated window where it is held in position.
references: AW189 RFM Section 7 — Indicating/Recording, Chap 31 (p.7-164)

items.question: Which door groups does the AW189 have?
options: Cockpit doors, passenger cabin doors, cargo compartment doors, and service and miscellaneous doors.
Cockpit doors and passenger cabin doors only, with all other openings classed as panels.
Cockpit, cabin, baggage and emergency exit doors.
Crew doors, sliding cabin doors and the rear clamshell doors.
items.explanation: The helicopter has cockpit doors, passenger cabin doors, cargo compartment doors, and service and miscellaneous doors.
references: AW189 RFM Section 7 — Doors, Chap 52 (p.7-359)

items.question: How is AW189 door status shown on the MFD?
options: On the PWR PLANT page as a helicopter silhouette with a line at each door position — amber when a microswitch detects the door open, green when closed.
As a list of door names that turn red when any door is open.
Only on the CAS — the MFD carries no door indication.
As a silhouette where an open door is shown by a flashing red line and a closed one by no line at all.
items.explanation: On the MFD PWR PLANT page the helicopter door status is displayed by a helicopter silhouette with amber or green lines corresponding to the door installation. Whenever a door microswitch detects a door open status it signals the Aircraft and Mission Management Computers to alert the crew with an amber line; door closed status is shown by a green line.
references: AW189 RFM Section 7 — Doors, Chap 52 (p.7-359)

items.question: What kind of engine control system does the AW189 use?
options: A dual-channel Full Authority Digital Electrical Control system, made up of an Engine Electronic Control Unit and a Fuel Management Unit.
A single-channel FADEC with a mechanical hydromechanical backup unit.
A hydromechanical fuel control with electronic supervisory trimming.
A dual-channel analogue electronic control with manual fuel governing.
items.explanation: The engines are equipped with a dual-channel Full Authority Digital Electrical Control (FADEC) system. The FADEC system is composed of the Engine Electronic Control Unit (EECU) and a Fuel Management Unit (FMU).
references: AW189 RFM Section 7 — Engine Controls, Chap 76 (p.7-423)

items.question: What authority does the AW189 EECU have over the engine?
options: It contains all computations and control laws and has full authority to vary all control inputs to the engine throughout their full range.
It trims the hydromechanical unit within a limited authority band of about 10 per cent.
It has full authority only above flight idle; below that the FMU governs mechanically.
It has authority over fuel flow only, with variable geometry controlled mechanically.
items.explanation: The EECU contains all computations and control laws and has the full authority to vary all control inputs to the engine throughout their full range.
references: AW189 RFM Section 7 — Engine Controls, Chap 76 (p.7-423)

items.question: What does the AW189 engine power control system consist of?
options: Two Electronic Engine Control Units, two Fuel Management Units and the engine control panel.
One EECU per engine and a shared fuel management unit.
Two EECUs, two FMUs and the collective LVDTs, with no separate control panel.
Two FMUs and the engine control panel — the EECUs are part of the AMMS.
items.explanation: The engine power control system includes the two Electronic Engine Control Units (EECU), the two Fuel Management Units (FMU) and the engine control panel. The control panel inputs manual commands while the EECU carries out the commands and normal operation automatically without operator intervention.
references: AW189 RFM Section 7 — Engine Controls, Chap 76 (p.7-423)

items.question: What are the two LVDTs at the left end of the AW189 collective torsion tube for?
options: They provide collective lever position to the engines and the AFCS, and are used to give the engines power anticipation.
They measure collective friction so the AFCS can compensate for it.
They provide collective position to the flight data recorder only.
They drive the collective trim actuator to hold the selected position.
items.explanation: Two Linear Variable Differential Transformers are installed at the left end of the collective torsion tube. They provide the position of the collective lever to the engines and the AFCS, and are used to provide power anticipation to the engine.
references: AW189 RFM Section 7 — Engine Controls, Chap 76 (p.7-423)

items.question: What does each AW189 EECU control, and how?
options: Together with its FMU and a network of sensors, it controls the engine gas generator and power turbine speeds in response to the load demanded by the rotor system.
It controls fuel flow only, with power turbine speed governed by the rotor brake logic.
It controls gas generator speed only; power turbine speed is set mechanically by the FMU.
It controls the variable geometry and start bleed valve, with fuel scheduled by the AMMS.
items.explanation: Each EECU is a dual-channel digital electronic unit that, together with the related FMU and a network of sensors, controls the engine gas generator and power turbine speeds in response to the load demanded by the rotor system.
references: AW189 RFM Section 7 — Engine Controls, Chap 76 (p.7-423)

items.question: How do the AW189 engine control panel and EECU connect to the rest of the aircraft?
options: Through the Aircraft and Mission Management System, for indicating, control and monitoring purposes.
Directly to the primary flight displays, bypassing the mission computers.
Through the electrical power generation and distribution system only.
They are standalone and exchange no data with aircraft systems.
items.explanation: Both the control panel and the EECU integrate with the aircraft systems by means of the Aircraft and Mission Management System (AMMS) for indicating, control and monitoring purposes.
references: AW189 RFM Section 7 — Engine Controls, Chap 76 (p.7-423)
